title: Find the Power of K-Size Subarrays II
statement:
Slide a window of `k` adjacent elements across the integer array `nums`. A window's power is its maximum when, read left to right, every element is exactly one more than the element before it (like `4, 5, 6`); any other window has power `-1`. A window of a single element always passes the test.

Return an array of length `nums.length - k + 1` listing the powers of all windows in order of their first index, so that entry `i` is the power of `nums[i..i + k - 1]`.
notes:
## Intuition

Checking the `k - 1` neighbouring pairs of every window costs O(n·k), far too slow when both are near 10^5. Notice instead that a window passes exactly when it sits inside one *climbing run*, a stretch where each value is the previous one plus 1. So for the window that ends at index `right` we only need the length of the climbing run ending there: if that run is at least `k` long it covers the whole window, and the window's maximum is its last value, `nums[right]`.

## Approach

1. Keep `streak`, the length of the climbing run that ends at index `right`.
2. Move `right` across `nums`. If `nums[right]` equals `nums[right - 1] + 1`, the run grows by one; otherwise a new run of length 1 starts at `right`.
3. Once `right >= k - 1`, the window `nums[right - k + 1..right]` is complete: push `nums[right]` if `streak >= k`, otherwise `-1`.
4. Windows complete in order of their first index, so `results` is already in the required order.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1,2,3,4,3,2,5]`, `k = 3`.

| `right` | `nums[right]` | `streak` | window | pushed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | 1 | not complete | |
| 1 | 2 | 2 | not complete | |
| 2 | 3 | 3 | `[1,2,3]` | `3` |
| 3 | 4 | 4 | `[2,3,4]` | `4` |
| 4 | 3 | 1 | `[3,4,3]` | `-1` |
| 5 | 2 | 1 | `[4,3,2]` | `-1` |
| 6 | 5 | 1 | `[3,2,5]` | `-1` |

The answer is `[3,4,-1,-1,-1]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each index is visited once with O(1) work.
- Space: O(1) besides the returned array.

## Pitfalls

- Increasing is not enough: `[1,3,5]` and `[2,2,3]` are in order but do not step by exactly 1.
- After a break, set `streak` to 1, not 0: the element that breaks the old run starts the next one. That is also why `k = 1` returns `nums` unchanged.
- A run longer than `k` covers several windows, so test `streak >= k`, not `streak === k`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `results` | the powers of the windows completed so far |
| `streak` | length of the climbing run that ends at `right` |
| `right` | last index of the current window |

narration.2: results collects one power per window, in order of the window's first index.
narration.3: streak will hold the length of the climbing run ending at the current index.
narration.4: Slide the window's last index right across the array.
narration.5: Is this value exactly one more than the previous one, so the climbing run continues?
narration.6: Yes: the run ending here is one element longer.
narration.8: No (or this is the first element): a new run of length 1 starts here.
narration.10: From index k - 1 on, a full window of k elements ends at right.
narration.11: If the run covers all k elements the window climbs by 1 and its last value is its maximum; otherwise its power is -1.
narration.14: Return the powers of all nums.length - k + 1 windows.
